after reviewing these datasets, we note that some of them
are of receipt type [12], [13], others consider a variety of
forms [14], [15], which differ slightly from a regular machine
written invoice. In [16], the authors propose a large dataset of
10000 synthetic invoices, specifically tailored for document
analysis and understanding. However, these documents do not
always reflect real-world scenarios where invoices are often
photographed with mobile phones, introducing significant dis-
tortions. We also notice that many of the datasets lack the
presence of stamp and signature components.
In order to fill this gap and to effectively apply DL tech-
niques, we propose a novel, fully annotated dataset composed
of real machine written invoice documents with various im-
perfections, such as blurriness, class imbalance, low-quality
phone-shot images, and varying formats. In our case study, we
consider a machine written invoice document to be valid only
if it contains a stamp, a signature, and certain selected fields.
After collecting and annotating the dataset, we select the most
relevant DL-based approaches for implementation and bench-
marking. We progressively evaluate and improve the results
until obtaining a robust pipeline that maximizes accuracy and
reliability, while maintaining reasonable performance.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. In
Section II, we present the material considered and the methods
proposed. The results are reported and discussed in Section III,
while Section IV concludes the paper and discusses the future
perspectives.
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS
In this section, we present the materials, detailing the data
collection and processing pipeline, and then describe the meth-
ods, including the selection of the most recent and relevant
models for implementation. Since invoice validation consists
of two main tasks, we divide our work into two independent
steps: keyword detection and object detection. The adopted
training pipeline is shown in Figure 1, which shows that
keyword detection is preceded by an OCR phase, which allows
for an OCR-augmented dataset. For object detection, we aim
to verify the presence of signatures and stamps to ensure the
authenticity of financial documents.
Fig. 1: Adopted training pipeline.
A. Materials
We outline the dataset used for our DL pipeline by first
describing the data annotation process, followed by data
augmentation and preparation.
1) Data annotation:
We collected 381 real financial documents, of which 84%
(320 documents) are invoices. Among these, 240 are machine-
written. We manually annotated the documents with bounding
boxes around the necessary elements to establish the validity
of the invoices, as shown in Table I. All classes are represented
as bounding boxes, except for a boolean attribute indicating
whether handwriting is present.
TABLE I: Annotated dataset description.
Class
Description
Title
Document type (e.g., invoice, receipt, etc.).
Client
Client name.
Stamp
Stamp for document authenticity.
Signature
Signature for document authenticity.
Date
Issue date, different formats.
Total
Total label.
Total Value
Total numeric value.
Handwritten
True if handwritten (not machine-written).
An example of an annotated document is shown in Figure
2. For confidentiality reasons, some parts of the financial
documents have been blurred.
Fig. 2: Example of an annotated document.
Our dataset includes various real invoices; many are dis-
torted due to mobile phone capture as depicted in Figure 3, and
some are handwritten, potentially appearing skewed during
capture, as illustrated by Figure 4.
This work focuses on the processing of digital invoices,
since handwritten invoices are sparse in the current dataset, and
present additional challenges for augmentation and processing.
